title: "Does ‘her offspring’ predict the virgin birth?"
description: "A fair examination of the claim that Genesis 3:15 predicts Jesus' virgin birth."

summary: "Christians have called Genesis 3:15 the first gospel. But does its reference to the woman's offspring actually predict a virgin birth?"
ot_reference: "Gen 3:15"
ot_text: "And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.”"
ot_note: "Or He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel. The same Hebrew root for crush, bruise, or strike appears twice in this verse."
christian_case: "Many Christians read this as the Bible's first promise of a deliverer. The serpent has brought sin and death into the story, but a future offspring of the woman will strike its head. Some evangelical interpreters argue that the singular grammar and the developing ‘seed’ theme in Genesis point toward one representative victor. Read alongside Matthew's account of Jesus' conception by the Holy Spirit and Paul's description of him as ‘born of a woman,’ the unusual phrase ‘her seed’ is then taken as a veiled anticipation of the virgin birth. This is a cumulative Christian reading: no single phrase carries the whole case."
critical_case: "The narrower virgin-birth claim goes beyond what Genesis says. The verse contrasts the woman with the serpent and her offspring with the serpent's; it never says that the offspring has no human father. Genesis itself speaks of Hagar's offspring (16:10) and Rebekah's offspring (24:60) without implying miraculous conception. The Hebrew word can refer collectively to descendants, and even an individual reading would identify a future person—not the manner of his conception. Neither Galatians 4:4 nor Matthew 1:18 cites Genesis 3:15. Later Christian texts and Eve–Mary typology can give the verse a meaningful canonical role, but that is different from finding the virgin birth predicted in its original wording."
verdict_label: "Later typology, not a virgin-birth prediction"
verdict: "Genesis 3:15 can support a Christian messianic or typological reading. Its wording does not independently predict a virgin birth; virgin conception is explicit in the later birth narratives, not in the phrase ‘her offspring.’"
